reason: I'll strengthen the bones first; the picture shows spaces for mineral in the living framework.
expectation: The mineral will fill those spaces and make the bones better able to resist compression.

alternatives.reason: Building the front muscle also fits a goal, but I want to strengthen the framework first.

effect: The bones are strengthened while the joint stays movable; next I'll build a muscle.
reaction: It's helpful to see that the mineral doesn't harden the joint too.
reason: I'll place muscle cells at the front attachments to start building one side of the elbow.
expectation: I expect a muscle to form between the front tendons, though I'm not sure how the cells assemble.

alternatives.reason: The back attachments also need muscle, but I'll start with the front.

effect: The front cells formed the biceps, whose pull bends the elbow; the back attachments still need muscle.
reaction: The arrows make the connection between attachment and movement clear.
reason: I'll use the only available combination to build muscle on the back of the elbow.
expectation: I expect a back muscle to form and pull the forearm in the opposite direction.

effect: The triceps completes the opposite side and shows that the same kind of muscle cell can straighten rather than bend the elbow because of where it attaches.
reaction: The matching arrows made the contrast with the biceps clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Building the muscles on opposite sides was most worthwhile: their pull arrows showed how attachment position changes the elbow's movement.

leastWorthwhile.text: Placing the second muscle was the least engaging choice because it was the only available combination, even though its result completed the comparison.

surprise.text: I hadn't expected the same kind of muscle cells to produce opposite movements just by attaching on different sides.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt especially arbitrary; the pictures showed spaces for mineral and muscle cells. I followed the offered pairings rather than independently discovering compatibility.

continue.text: Yes, I'd try another chapter: seeing the same cells make opposing movements made me curious about how other body parts work together.
